title: How to Turn an Android Tablet Into a Digital Photo Frame
content: How to turn an Android tablet into a digital photo frameUpdated August 9, 2026 · 10 min readBuying a dedicated digital photo frame means paying for locked-down hardware with limited source options and recurring subscription fees. An Android tablet you already own — or one you can pick up cheaply — gives you far more control: any photo source, any layout, scheduled playback, weather overlays, and no annual fee.Which Android tablets work bestAlmost any Android tablet running Android 8 or later works. For a dedicated always-on frame the key specs are screen quality and charging stability, not processing power. Good options across price ranges:  Amazon Fire tablets (HD 8, HD 10): Inexpensive, widely available, and supported via the Amazon Appstore. Good for fixed wall or shelf mounting. Fire OS works well for always-on use.  Samsung Galaxy Tab A series: Reliable build quality, good display brightness, and standard Android that supports the full Google ecosystem including Google Photos.  Lenovo Tab series: Competitive pricing with solid displays. Good for budget builds.  Old tablets you already own: A tablet that is too slow for general use often still has a perfectly capable display. Dedicated frame use is not demanding.Hardware setup  Choose your location first. Decide whether the tablet will sit on a shelf, stand on a desk, or mount on a wall. Route your power cable before committing to a position.  Get a stand or mount. For shelf or desk: any tablet stand works. For walls: adhesive mounts or slim VESA adapters designed for tablets keep cables hidden.  Use a permanent power source. The tablet should stay plugged in. Use a short, right-angle USB cable to keep the connection tidy and reduce stress on the port.  Disable battery optimisation for the frame app. Go to Android Settings → Apps → Fravora → Battery → Unrestricted. This prevents the system from killing the app during idle periods.  Disable screen timeout. The frame app handles screen-on state via its own Keep Screen Awake setting. You can also set the system display timeout to the maximum or use Developer Options to keep the screen awake while charging.App setup in FravoraWhen you first launch Fravora, the onboarding walks you through choosing a photo source — local folders, Google Photos, NAS, Immich, or any other supported type — and creating your first album. Your frame is already showing photos by the time onboarding finishes. After that, fine-tune the display settings:  Enable Fullscreen Mode in Settings → Appearance to hide the status bar and navigation buttons for a clean display.  Enable Keep Screen Awake in Settings → Appearance so the display stays on during slideshow hours.  Set Running Hours in Settings → Slideshow so the frame wakes and sleeps on your schedule. Outside those hours the screen shows a standby clock or goes black.  To add more photo sources or source types, go to Settings → Sources.Choosing your photo sourcesThe right source depends on where your photos live. You can use any combination:  Local device folders: Copy photos to the tablet's storage or SD card and add those folders as sources. Completely offline, no accounts needed.  Google Photos: Use the official Google Photos Picker to select which photos appear on the frame. Photos are cached locally and display without a live internet connection once downloaded.  NAS / SMB network share: Connect directly to a Synology, QNAP, or Windows share on your home network. Photos stay on your NAS and are served over Wi-Fi.  OneDrive, Dropbox, or Immich: Pick specific cloud folders or Immich albums as sources. Useful if your photo library lives in another cloud service.Display and overlay settingsFravora gives you control over what appears on top of photos. Useful settings for a home display:  Clock overlay: Shows the current time. Position it in any corner at small, medium, or large size.  Weather overlay (PRO): Shows current temperature and conditions. Requires GPS permission or a manually set location.  Photo metadata (PRO): Shows when and where a photo was taken, with landmark name lookup for travel photos.  Display Mode: Choose Fit (full photo visible) or Fill (zoom to cover the full screen). In Fit mode, choose a backdrop style — Mirrored or Gradient — to fill the letterbox area.Transition and motion effects (PRO)The free tier uses a hard cut between photos. PRO adds ten transition styles including Crossfade, Slide, Cube, and Parallax, plus cinematic motion effects — Ken Burns pan-and-zoom, Drift, and Vignette Pulse — that keep static photos feeling alive. Transition speed is also configurable.OLED burn-in protectionIf your tablet has an OLED display, leaving static overlays in the same position 24/7 can cause image retention. Fravora's Anti-burn-in overlay effect (PRO) periodically micro-shifts overlay positions and varies their opacity. The Bouncing standby clock (PRO) prevents burn-in from a fixed clock position during off-hours.  Amazon Fire tablet notes  Fire tablets run Fire OS, a modified Android fork. Fravora is available on the Amazon Appstore and supports all core features on Fire OS. Google Photos requires signing into a Google account, which Fire tablets support via a standard browser login during the Google Photos Picker flow. NAS/SMB connections work normally over Wi-Fi. Voice control using wake-word detection also works on Fire tablets.  Keeping the frame running long-term  The most common failure mode for always-on frames is the app being killed by the system. To prevent this: grant the frame app unrestricted battery access, disable any power-saving modes that restrict background apps, and set Fravora as the device's home app if you want it to restart automatically after a reboot. Use the running-hours schedule to give the device rest periods, which also extends display life.  Get Fravora  All features  Setup walkthrough  Google Photos guide  NAS photo frame guide

content: Digital photo frame with internet radio: setup and featuresUpdated August 10, 2026 · 7 min readMost digital photo frames are silent. Tap it to toggle play/pause, double-tap to open station search  Station failure info: If a stream fails, the app shows the specific reason — timeout, access denied, unsupported format — so you can find a better stream quicklySetup: what the onboarding coversWhen you first launch Fravora, the onboarding guides you through your photo sources and first album. Radio is set up separately after onboarding:  Open Settings → Audio and tap the Radio tab  Search for a station by name or genre and tap it to start playing  The station plays immediately alongside the slideshowTo save stations for quick access later and enable features like background playback and lockscreen controls, upgrade to PRO.Free vs PRO for radioThe free tier lets you search, select, and play any station during the current session. The station is remembered while the app is open but cleared on restart. PRO adds:  Station persistence: Your last station is remembered across restarts  Favorites: Save stations for one-tap access without searching again  Recently played: Quick history of the last 3 stations  Advanced search filters: Filter by country, language, genre tag, and minimum bitrate  Background playback: Radio keeps playing when the screen turns off or another app comes to the foreground  Lockscreen controls: Play/pause and switch stations from the Android notification shade without opening the app  Audio Running Hours: Set a separate schedule for when radio auto-starts and stops, independent of the slideshow schedule  Now Playing overlay: The scrolling station and track name marquee on top of photosLocal music playlistsIf you prefer your own music library over internet radio, the Music tab in the same Audio section lets you create folder-based playlists from device storage or SD card. Add whole folders recursively and the app scans for mp3, flac, aac, ogg, opus, wav, and m4a files. Free tier supports one playlist; PRO unlocks unlimited playlists, automatic background rescans, and full sort modes including shuffle.Separate audio and slideshow schedulesOne detail worth knowing: the audio running hours are independent of the slideshow running hours. You can keep music playing in the morning while photos are still in standby, or stop audio earlier than the frame display. Both are configured under Settings → Audio and Settings → Slideshow respectively.  Connecting a Bluetooth speaker  If the tablet's built-in speaker is not loud enough for a room, connect a Bluetooth speaker. Fravora includes a Preferred Bluetooth Device setting under Audio that lets you select a specific paired device for playback, so the app always routes audio to the right speaker without manual switching each time.  Kitchen and living room setups  A common use case is a kitchen tablet that shows family photos and plays a morning radio station. The frame wakes on schedule, starts the slideshow, and auto-plays the last radio station. The now-playing overlay shows the current track, the ambient logo pulses with the music, and the whole thing runs without any interaction needed. If you want to skip a station or pause, the ambient logo tap controls work from across the room, or voice commands can handle it if enabled. title: How to Add Weather to a Digital Photo Frame on Android
content: How to add weather to a digital photo frame on AndroidUpdated August 9, 2026 · 7 min readA digital photo frame that also shows the weather is more useful than one that only displays photos — especially in a kitchen or hallway where you glance at it throughout the day. Fravora's weather overlay puts the current temperature and conditions directly on the frame screen alongside your photos, and tapping it opens a full hourly and 7-day forecast without leaving the frame.What the weather overlay shows  Current temperature in Celsius or Fahrenheit (your choice)  Current conditions with an adaptive weather icon (clear, cloudy, rain, snow, etc.)  Overlay size: Small, Medium, or Large — readable from across a room  Position: assignable to any corner or center slot via the Overlay Layout gridSetup: what the onboarding coversWhen you first launch Fravora, the onboarding walks you through adding photo sources and creating your first album. After your frame is running, enable the weather overlay from Settings:  Open Settings → Overlays.  Enable the Weather toggle.  Grant location permission when prompted. Fravora uses GPS to determine your location for local weather data. A warning icon appears if weather is enabled without location permission.  Choose your preferred temperature unit (Celsius or Fahrenheit) and overlay size.  Optionally open Overlay Layout to move the weather widget to a different corner — by default it appears in the top-left, but you can place it in any of the four corners or center slots.To add more overlays or rearrange their positions later, go to Settings → Overlays → Overlay Layout.Tapping the weather overlay: full-screen forecastTapping the weather widget on the frame screen opens a full-screen weather forecast without interrupting the slideshow. The forecast view includes:  24-hour hourly strip — temperature and conditions for each hour through the next day, with midnight wrap labels  7-day daily forecast — day/night temperature range, precipitation probability, and condition icons  Swipe navigation — swipe left and right within the hour or day detail views to move through the forecast range  Rich detail per slot — temperature, precipitation probability, wind speed, humidity, and UV index  Localized labels — hour and day labels follow your configured clock and date formatClosing the forecast returns you to the slideshow exactly where it left off.Combining weather with other overlaysThe weather overlay shares the screen with other overlays — clock, photo metadata, now-playing, and photo index. The Overlay Layout grid lets you assign each overlay to a specific corner or center slot so they don't overlap. A common setup for a kitchen frame: weather in the top-left, clock in the bottom-right, and now-playing (if you use radio) at the bottom-center.The anti-burn-in effect (PRO) periodically micro-shifts all overlay positions and varies their opacity, which protects OLED screens from image retention caused by static weather and clock widgets sitting in the same spot all day.Weather and the photo metadata overlayIf you also enable the photo metadata overlay (PRO), the frame can show both weather and the capture location of each photo simultaneously. A travel photo from Japan can show "Shibuya, Tokyo" as the photo label while your current local weather sits in a separate corner — the two overlays coexist without interfering.  Placement tips for weather-forward setups  Kitchen: Place weather in the top-left corner at Medium or Large size so it is readable from the counter or table without walking up to the device.  Bedroom: Use Small size and position it in a corner away from the clock. The forecast tap is useful for a quick morning check before getting up.  Office or hallway: Weather at Large size in a top corner is visible from a distance and does not require interaction unless you want the full forecast detail.  Privacy note  Fravora uses GPS location only for weather data — it does not store, transmit, or log your location to any external service beyond the weather API request. Location is read locally on the device and used only to fetch a weather response.  Get Fravora  All features  User manual  Tablet setup guide  Google Photos guide

title: Digital Photo Frame Glossary: NAS, SMB, Immich, and More
content: Digital photo frame glossary  Plain-language explanations of the technical terms that come up when setting up an Android digital photo frame. Each entry links to the relevant Fravora feature or guide where applicable.      NAS Network Attached Storage    A NAS is a storage device connected to your home network that other devices — including phones, computers, and photo frames — can access over Wi-Fi or Ethernet. Common NAS brands include Synology, QNAP, and TrueNAS. Using a NAS as a photo frame source means your photos never leave your home network and you are not limited by cloud storage quotas. Fravora connects to NAS devices via SMB. See the NAS photo frame setup guide.        SMB Server Message Block    SMB is the network file-sharing protocol used by Windows, Synology, QNAP, TrueNAS, and most NAS devices. When Fravora connects to a "network share," it is using SMB to browse folders and download photos over your local network. No internet connection is required — SMB works entirely within your home network. Fravora supports credential formats including DOMAIN\user and user@domain.        Immich    Immich is a self-hosted photo and video management application — essentially a private Google Photos that runs on hardware you own (a home server, NAS, Raspberry Pi, or VPS). Immich organises photos into albums and provides a mobile app for uploading and browsing. Fravora connects to Immich servers using a URL and API key, letting you use your Immich albums as photo frame sources. See the Immich photo frame guide.        EXIF data    EXIF (Exchangeable Image File Format) is metadata embedded in photo files by cameras and smartphones. It typically includes the date and time the photo was taken, the camera model, exposure settings, and GPS coordinates if location was enabled. Fravora's photo metadata overlay reads EXIF data to display when and where a photo was taken directly on the frame. The location coordinates are reverse-geocoded to show a city name or landmark.        Ken Burns effect    A slow pan-and-zoom motion applied to a still photo, named after the documentary filmmaker who popularised it. On a photo frame it makes static images feel alive — the camera slowly zooms in and pans across the photo during the display interval. Fravora implements Ken Burns as a cinematic effect with a randomised 1.05–1.15× zoom range. It is a PRO feature available alongside Drift (pan-only) and Vignette Pulse.        OLED burn-in    OLED displays produce light at the pixel level, and pixels that display the same content continuously can degrade faster than surrounding pixels, leaving a faint permanent "ghost" of that image — this is called burn-in. For a photo frame with a fixed clock or weather overlay in the same corner all day, burn-in is a real risk over months of use. Fravora addresses this with two features: a bouncing standby clock during off-hours that moves the display around the screen, and an anti-burn-in overlay effect (PRO) that periodically micro-shifts overlay positions and varies their opacity.        Album (Fravora)    In Fravora, an album is a named collection of photo source assignments that play together as a slideshow. One album might combine a NAS folder, a Google Photos pick set, and a local device folder — all rotating together. You can have multiple albums and switch between them, or enable multiple albums to play sequentially. Albums are created and managed under Settings → Albums.        Overlay    An overlay is information displayed on top of the photo while the slideshow is running — without interrupting it. Fravora's overlays include the clock, weather, photo metadata (date and location), now-playing (radio/music station and track), photo index (current / total count), and the ambient logo. Each overlay can be positioned independently in a corner or center slot using the Overlay Layout grid. Overlays can be enabled, disabled, and resized independently.        Running hours    Running hours is a scheduled on/off window for the frame — the hours during which it displays photos. Outside the running hours, the frame enters standby: it either shows a large clock or goes fully black, but remains tappable to reach the menu. Fravora supports a simple start/end time for all days, or a custom per-day schedule. Separate running hours can be set for the slideshow and for audio (radio or music).        SAF Storage Access Framework    SAF is Android's built-in system for granting apps access to files and folders without giving blanket storage permission. When Fravora asks you to "Add Folder" for local sources or music playlists, it opens the Android file picker — that picker is SAF. SAF permissions are persistent: once you grant access to a folder, the app retains that access until you remove it, even across reboots. This is how Fravora can scan local folders and music libraries in the background without requiring broad storage access.        Smart Shuffle    A PRO photo ordering mode in Fravora that improves on random shuffle by reducing back-to-back similar photos. It detects burst-style filenames (sequences of photos taken within seconds of each other) and similar capture timestamps, spacing them out across the rotation so the slideshow feels more varied. Standard random shuffle does not account for these patterns, which can cause the same event or burst sequence to appear clustered together.        Google Photos Picker    The official Android system interface for selecting photos from Google Photos without giving an app access to your full library. When Fravora connects to Google Photos, it uses the Picker: you choose specific photos or albums, and only those selections are accessible to the app. Your full Google Photos library remains private. The Picker approach is more private than older Google Photos API integrations that required broad library access. No per-device limits: Unlike Google Photos with its storage quotas, your Immich library is limited only by your own storage hardware.  Works on your local network: The frame connects to your Immich server over Wi-Fi. No internet connection is required if the server is on your home network.What you need before connecting  A running Immich server accessible by URL from the Android device (local IP, hostname, or domain)  An Immich API key — generate one in Immich under Account Settings → API Keys  At least one Immich album containing the photos you want on the frame  An Android tablet or display device running FravoraSetup: what the onboarding coversWhen you first launch Fravora, the onboarding guides you through connecting your first source. Here is what it covers for an Immich connection:  Choose Immich as your source type.  Enter your Immich server URL. For a local server this is typically http://192.168.x.x:2283 or http://immich.local:2283. For an externally accessible server, use your domain with HTTPS.  Paste your Immich API key into the API Key field.  Tap Test Connection. Fravora contacts your server, verifies the key, and confirms access before saving.  The album picker opens. Select the Immich album or albums you want displayed on the frame.  Name your slideshow album and assign the Immich source to it. The frame begins downloading and displaying your photos — setup is done.To add more Immich connections or other source types later, go to Settings → Sources.How to generate an Immich API key  Open your Immich web interface and log in.  Click your avatar in the top-right corner and go to Account Settings.  Scroll to the API Keys section and click New API Key.  Give it a name (e.g. "Photo Frame") and copy the generated key. You will only see the key once — paste it into Fravora immediately.Caching and offline behaviourFravora caches downloaded Immich photos on the device using the standard image cache (configurable from 128 MB to 2 GB). Once a photo is cached, it displays without contacting the server. This means short network outages — a router reboot, a NAS going to sleep, a brief Wi-Fi drop — do not interrupt the slideshow. The frame picks up new photos from Immich on the next scheduled scan.Mixing Immich with other sourcesImmich does not have to be your only photo source. A single Fravora album can combine Immich album targets with local device folders, NAS/SMB shares, Google Photos picks, OneDrive folders, and Dropbox folders. All sources rotate together in the slideshow. A common setup for self-hosters is Immich for recently imported photos plus a NAS SMB share for the older organised archive — both playing from the same frame.Recommended album strategyRather than pointing the frame at your entire Immich library, create a dedicated Frame album in Immich and curate it. Add photos you want displayed, remove ones you do not. This keeps the slideshow intentional — not a raw dump of every camera import — and makes it easy to update what the frame shows without touching the frame app itself. You can add more albums from Immich as additional sources within the same Fravora album if you want broader coverage.  Common Immich server setups that work  Synology NAS with Docker: Run Immich in Docker Compose on a Synology NAS. The frame connects via the NAS local IP and the Immich port. This is one of the most popular self-hosting setups and works reliably on the local network.  QNAP with Container Station: Similar to Synology — deploy Immich containers via Container Station and connect via local IP.  TrueNAS SCALE: Immich can be deployed as a TrueNAS application. The frame connects via the TrueNAS host IP and Immich's port.  Raspberry Pi or home server: A bare-metal Linux server running Immich works the same way. Use the server's local IP address as the connection URL.  VPS with a public domain: If your Immich server is accessible on the internet via a domain with HTTPS, the frame can connect from anywhere — useful if the frame is on a different network from the server, such as a frame at a relative's house showing your photos.  Troubleshooting connection issues  Test Connection fails: Double-check the URL format — include the port number if Immich is not on port 80 or 443. Confirm the API key was copied correctly with no trailing spaces. If your server uses a self-signed certificate, make sure the Android device trusts it or use HTTP on a local network.  Photos not appearing: Confirm the selected albums contain photos and the API key user has access to those albums. In Immich, album visibility is per-user — the API key inherits the permissions of the account it belongs to. Network Shares (SMB / NAS)                  Host/share format is hostname/sharename (no smb:// prefix required).          Test connection checks host/share path and credentials before saving.          Username and password are optional, including guest access and domain-qualified users.          After connecting, select one or more folders from the share to activate it. Local Folders        Add folders from internal storage, SD card, or USB media using Android's system picker. Fravora stores only the access grants required for playback. Low Storage Alert: warns when configured cache exceeds available storage.          Scan Interval (PRO): 5 to 120 minutes for periodic source refreshes. Clear Cache: available for image cache and Google Photos cache.                                🖼️ Albums      Albums are the playback collections Fravora scans for slideshow images. Enable Voice Control and complete the first-time safety disclaimer acknowledgement. title: NAS and SMB Photo Frame on Android: Complete Setup Guide
content: NAS and SMB photo frame on AndroidUpdated August 9, 2026 · 9 min readIf you store photos on a home NAS — Synology, QNAP, TrueNAS, or a plain Windows share — you can display them directly on an Android digital photo frame over your local network using SMB. No cloud upload required, no subscription, and your photos never leave your home network.Why NAS is the best source for a home photo frame  Privacy: Photos are served from your own hardware. Nothing goes to a third-party server.  No storage limits: A NAS can hold hundreds of thousands of photos. The frame scans and rotates through them without any per-device cap.  Single source of truth: Your organised folder structure on the NAS is exactly what the frame sees — no duplicate library to maintain.  Offline resilience: If your internet goes down, the frame keeps running because the NAS is local.Compatible NAS devices and setupsAny device that supports SMB file sharing works. Common setups that have been tested and work well:  Synology DiskStation (DSM) — enable the SMB service in Control Panel → File Services  QNAP NAS — enable Samba (SMB) in Control Panel → Network & File Services  TrueNAS / FreeNAS — add an SMB share via the Sharing menu  Windows PC — right-click a folder, Properties → Sharing → Share  Linux with Samba — configure smb.conf and share the photo directorySetup: what the onboarding coversWhen you first launch Fravora, the onboarding guides you through connecting your first source. Here is what it covers for a NAS setup:  Choose Network share (SMB/NAS) as your source type.  Enter the NAS address (IP or hostname), share name, and credentials. Fravora supports both DOMAIN\user and user@domain credential formats.  Tap Test Connection to verify the credentials and path before saving.  Use the Folder Picker to browse your share and select the folders you want in the slideshow. System folders like @Recycle, @eaDir, and .Trash are automatically hidden.  Name your album and assign the NAS folder targets to it.  The frame starts scanning and displaying your NAS photos — setup is done.To add more shares or other source types later, go to Settings → Sources.Handling network outagesNAS connections occasionally drop — router reboots, NAS sleep cycles, or brief network hiccups. Fravora handles this without interrupting playback:  Local cache: All SMB images are cached on the device. The slideshow continues from cache during outages.  Non-blocking warning: A small warning icon appears in the notification strip if a share is unreachable, but playback continues on available photos.  NAS reconnect interval: Configure how often the app retries a failed share (1, 5, 10, 15, 30, or 60 minutes, or never). Once reconnected, the scan resumes automatically.  SMB retry count: Set how many connection attempts the app makes per operation (3 to 7 retries). Useful for shares that take a moment to wake from standby.  Full blocking overlay: Only appears if every source fails and zero cached photos are available — includes a Retry button and direct link to Sources settings.Folder organisation and scanningYou can select multiple folders from the same share and combine them in a single album. Scanning is recursive by default on PRO — the app walks into subfolders automatically. On the free tier, scanning is folder-level only (subfolders are a PRO feature). New photos added to the NAS folders are picked up automatically on the next scan.Configure how often the app scans for new content under Settings → Sources → Scan Interval (PRO). The free tier uses a fixed default interval.Mixing NAS with other sourcesYou are not limited to NAS only. A single album can combine NAS folder targets with local device folders, Google Photos picks, OneDrive folders, and Immich albums. All sources play together in the rotation. If the NAS goes down temporarily, photos from other sources continue displaying.  Synology-specific tips  On Synology DSM, make sure SMB is enabled and the connecting user has read permissions on the shared folder. If you use a dedicated Synology user for the frame, grant it read-only access — this limits what the app can access if the credentials are ever compromised. Use the IP address of the NAS rather than its hostname if DNS resolution is unreliable on your network.  QNAP-specific tips  On QNAP, enable Samba in Network & File Services → Win/Mac/NFS → Microsoft Networking. Make sure the shared folder's permissions include the user account you are using. If the NAS uses a non-standard SMB port, enter it in the host field as ip:port.  Get Fravora  All features  User manual  Google Photos guide  Tablet setup guide

title: Self-Hosted Photo Frame: Immich vs. Local SMB Compared | Fravora Blog
content: Self-Hosted Photo Frame: Immich vs. Local SMB ComparedPublished August 20, 2026 · 8 min readPrivacy-conscious users are increasingly moving away from cloud-locked photo frames like Nixplay or Aura in favor of self-hosted solutions. For Android tablet users, the two most popular ways to feed a frame are Immich (API-based) and Local SMB/NAS (file-based). Here is how they compare and which one fits your setup.1. The Immich API ApproachImmich has quickly become the favorite open-source alternative to Google Photos. Fravora connects to your self-hosted Immich server using your URL and an API key. This approach is best if you already use Immich as your primary photo management tool.  Pros: Access to Immich's rich metadata, easy album-based selection, and high-performance loading over the API.  Cons: Requires an active Immich instance and a stable network connection to your server for initial syncs.2. The Local SMB / NAS ApproachThis is the "classic" way to run an offline photo frame. You share a folder on your Synology, QNAP, or Windows PC over the SMB protocol, and Fravora reads the files directly. This approach is best if your photos are just "files in folders" and you want maximum simplicity.  Pros: Works fully offline, no API management needed, and compatible with almost any networked storage.  Cons: Lacks the organizational features of a dedicated photo manager; you rely purely on folder structure.  Which one should you choose?  Choose Immich if: You want a Google Photos-like experience but on your own hardware. You enjoy using a web UI or mobile app to curate "Frame" albums that automatically sync to your device.  Choose SMB if: You just want to point Fravora at a /Photos folder on your NAS and let it run. It's the most resilient option for dedicated offline frames that might lose internet access for long periods.Mixing the Best of Both WorldsOne of Fravora's unique strengths is that you don't have to choose. A single album in Fravora can combine an Immich album, an SMB folder from your NAS, and even a local "Favorites" folder from your tablet's SD card. title: Synology NAS Digital Photo Frame on Android: Setup Guide
content: Synology NAS digital photo frame on AndroidUpdated August 10, 2026 · 8 min readIf your photos live on a Synology NAS, you can display them on an Android digital photo frame over your local network without uploading anything to the cloud. Fravora connects to Synology DiskStation devices via SMB — the same protocol Synology uses for Windows file sharing — and serves photos directly to the tablet's slideshow. Your photos stay on your NAS and never leave your home network.Why Synology + Android frame is a strong combination  No cloud dependency: SMB is a local network protocol. The connection works entirely within your home — no internet required, no third-party service in the path  No storage limits: Your Synology can hold terabytes of photos. The frame scans and rotates through all of them  Existing organisation respected: The folder structure you already maintain on the NAS is exactly what the frame sees. No duplicate library to manage  Works with Synology Photos: The shared folders that Synology Photos uses are standard SMB shares. Fravora can read them directlyStep 1: Enable SMB on your Synology NAS  Log into the Synology DSM web interface  Open Control Panel → File Services → SMB  Enable the SMB service and click Apply  Note your NAS's local IP address — you'll find it in Control Panel → Network → Network Interface or in your router's device list. It will look like 192.168.x.xStep 2: Create a dedicated user for the frame (recommended)Rather than using your admin account, create a read-only user specifically for the frame. This limits what the app can access if the credentials are ever compromised.  Open Control Panel → User & Group → Create  Create a user (e.g., frameuser) with a strong password  In the user's permissions, grant Read only access to the shared folders containing your photos  Disable access to all other shared folders and applicationsStep 3: Connect Fravora to your SynologyWhen you first launch Fravora, the onboarding guides you through adding your first source. Select Network share (SMB/NAS) and the connection flow covers all the steps below. To add more Synology shares later, go to Settings → Sources → Add network share.  Enter the NAS address: the IP address noted in Step 1 (e.g., 192.168.1.100). You can also use the Synology hostname if your router resolves it (e.g., DiskStation)  Enter the share name — the name of the shared folder as it appears in DSM File Station (e.g., photo or homes)  Enter the username and password for the frame user created in Step 2. Both DOMAIN\user and user@domain formats are supported if your NAS uses a domain  Tap Test Connection to verify before saving  Use the Folder Picker to browse the share and select the specific photo folders you want in the slideshow. Synology system folders like @eaDir and #recycle are automatically hiddenStep 4: Create an album and start the slideshow  In the onboarding (or later in Settings → Albums), assign your Synology folder targets to an album and name it  Enable the album and return to the slideshow  Fravora scans the selected folders and starts displaying your photosHandling NAS sleep and outagesSynology NAS devices can go into a low-power sleep state when idle. If the NAS is asleep when the frame tries to scan, Fravora treats it as a temporary outage: the slideshow continues from cached photos, a non-blocking warning icon appears in the notification strip, and the app retries automatically. Configure the retry interval (1/5/10/15/30/60 minutes) under Settings → Sources → NAS reconnect interval.If your Synology has HDD spin-down enabled, the first scan after a sleep period may take 10–30 seconds for the drives to spin up. Increase the SMB retry count (up to 7 retries) in Settings → Sources to handle this gracefully.  Using Synology as a music source too  Fravora can also play music from your Synology NAS. The Music tab in Settings → Audio supports adding NAS folders as music sources via high-performance SMB scanning. Your music library on the NAS is read directly — no syncing or copying to the tablet required. This works especially well for setups where the frame doubles as a kitchen or living room music player.  Mixing Synology with other sources  You are not limited to a single Synology share. One Fravora album can combine multiple Synology folders, a Google Photos pick set, an Immich album, and local device folders — all rotating together. A common setup: NAS share for the main photo archive, Google Photos for recent camera roll imports, all in one album. title: Voice-Controlled Digital Photo Frame on Android: What Works and What to Expect
content: Voice-controlled digital photo frame on Android: what works and what to expectUpdated August 10, 2026 · 7 min readA frame mounted on a kitchen wall or across the living room is inconvenient to interact with physically. Voice commands let you skip a photo, pause audio, or adjust the volume without walking over to the device. Fravora supports wake-word voice control on any Android tablet as a PRO feature — but it is important to understand what it can and cannot do before you set your expectations.The honest mic limitation: this is not Alexa  Fravora's voice control uses the tablet's built-in microphone, which is designed for video calls and voice memos at close range — not for far-field pickup across a room. It is not comparable to an Amazon Echo, Google Nest, or any purpose-built smart speaker. In a quiet room at a reasonable distance (a few metres) it works well. In a noisy environment or from the other side of a large room, recognition will be unreliable.With that framing set: for the right use case — a kitchen frame at counter distance, a bedroom frame you address from the bed, or a hallway frame you pass close to — voice control is a genuine convenience. It covers the moments where your hands are busy or you do not want to walk over to the device. It does not replace a smart speaker.What commands are availableAfter saying the wake phrase, Fravora listens for a command for 3 to 7 seconds (configurable). Available command categories:  Slideshow: "play slideshow", "pause slideshow", "stop slideshow" — and many equivalent phrasings  Radio and music: "play radio", "stop radio", "play music", "pause music" — and many equivalent phrasings. If no station is saved yet, the app opens the radio search automatically  Volume: "increase volume", "lower volume", "set volume to 50", "mute", "unmute" — volume adjusts in 5% steps for increase/decrease  Voice control itself: "stop voice control" immediately disables the feature for the sessionCommands must be spoken in English. The parser uses fuzzy matching, so variations like "turn on the radio" or "switch off the music" are recognised alongside the most direct phrasings.Wake phrasesChoose between "Hello Frame" or "Hello Fravora" as your wake phrase. Both use fuzzy matching to tolerate slight variations in pronunciation. A configurable audible chime plays when the wake word is detected so you know the app is listening. The frame border turns blue during the listening window, green on a successful command, and red if the command is not recognised.Setup: what the onboarding coversVoice control is enabled after the initial onboarding that sets up your photo sources and first album. To activate it:  Open Settings → Voice Control  Accept the activation disclaimer (a one-time 3-second acknowledgement lock)  Choose your wake phrase and enable the command categories you want  The frame immediately starts listening for the wake phrase in the backgroundYou can independently enable or disable the slideshow, audio, and volume command categories. If you only want volume control, you can leave the others off.Getting reliable recognitionBecause recognition depends on the device microphone, placement and environment matter more than they would with a dedicated smart speaker:  Distance: Works most reliably within 2–3 metres of the device. Recognition drops off past that on most tablet hardware  Background noise: Music playing from the frame itself competes with wake-word detection. Lower the volume if you are having difficulty triggering the wake phrase  Tablet microphone quality: Mid-range and higher Android tablets generally have better microphones than entry-level devices. If recognition is poor, this is the most likely cause — not the software  Command window: Set the command window to 5–7 seconds if you speak slowly or need time to form the command after the wake word  Show recognized text: Enable the speech recognition overlay in Settings → Voice Control to see what the app hears — useful for diagnosing why a command is not being recognised  Best use cases for frame voice control  Kitchen: Frame at counter height, 1–2 metres away. Hands are occupied with cooking. "Hello Frame, stop audio" or "Hello Frame, increase volume" works well without touching anything.  Bedroom: Frame on a dresser or nightstand. "Hello Frame, pause slideshow" before sleep, or "Hello Frame, play music" when you wake up, without reaching for the device.  Home office: Frame on a desk or shelf. Quick volume or audio control without breaking focus.  Less suitable: Large open-plan rooms where the frame is more than 3–4 metres away, or rooms with significant ambient noise from TV, appliances, or other people talking.
